reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Most common in infants and young children because of a shorter, more horizontal Eustachian tube; often follows an upper respiratory tract infection
Presents with ear pain, fever, irritability and conduction-type hearing loss; young children may only tug at the ear or feed poorly
Otoscopy progresses through stages: initial hyperaemia, then a bulging congested drum, then perforation with discharge, and finally resolution
Sudden relief of pain accompanied by ear discharge usually signals spontaneous perforation of the tympanic membrane
Common organisms include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis
Management principles centre on analgesia and appropriate antibiotics; myringotomy is considered when the drum is bulging, pain is severe, or complications threaten
Watchful waiting without immediate antibiotics may be appropriate in older children with mild, non-severe disease
Recurrent episodes or persistent effusion warrant assessment for adenoid hypertrophy and Eustachian tube dysfunction
reference.pathophysiology: Acute otitis media is an acute suppurative inflammation of the middle ear cleft, usually arising when Eustachian tube dysfunction (commonly from a viral upper respiratory infection or adenoid obstruction) impairs middle ear ventilation and drainage. Negative middle ear pressure and mucosal oedema allow pathogens to ascend from the nasopharynx and proliferate, producing an inflammatory exudate that becomes purulent. Rising pressure causes the tympanic membrane to bulge and may lead to necrosis and perforation with discharge, after which the process typically resolves. Untreated or aggressive infection can extend to adjacent structures.
additionalDifferentials: Referred otalgia from teeth, throat or temporomandibular joint
Furuncle of the external auditory canal
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy to assess drum colour, position, mobility and integrity
Tuning fork tests and audiometry to characterise conductive hearing loss
Tympanometry where effusion or Eustachian tube dysfunction is suspected
Culture of ear discharge in severe, recurrent or non-resolving cases
Imaging of the temporal bone if intratemporal or intracranial complications are suspected
redFlags: Postauricular swelling, tenderness or a protruding pinna suggesting acute mastoiditis
Persistent high fever, severe headache, neck stiffness or altered consciousness indicating intracranial spread
Facial nerve weakness or vertigo suggesting facial canal or labyrinthine involvement
Failure to improve despite adequate treatment
reference.prognosis: Most cases resolve completely with prompt treatment and restoration of normal hearing, but neglected or recurrent infection can progress to chronic otitis media, persistent effusion, or intratemporal and intracranial complications.
pitfalls: Mistaking otitis externa or referred otalgia for middle ear infection
Overlooking early mastoiditis in a child who is not improving
Assuming a red drum alone confirms the diagnosis without assessing bulging and mobility
Failing to follow up to ensure resolution of effusion and return of hearing
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Adequate analgesia and antipyresis with paracetamol or ibuprofen as first-line symptom control
Watchful waiting in otherwise well children with mild disease, reserving antibiotics for severe, bilateral, or non-resolving cases
Oral amoxicillin as first-line antibiotic, with co-amoxiclav for treatment failure or severe disease
Myringotomy for a bulging drum, severe pain, or threatened complications
Monitor for persistent effusion and conductive hearing loss after the acute episode
Watch for intratemporal and intracranial complications such as mastoiditis and refer urgently if they arise
ENT referral for recurrent episodes, with consideration of ventilation tubes (grommets)
